summary: A library roadmap in combinatorial and geometric group theory and algebraic geometry over groups, built on Mathlib's FreeGroup, amalgams (Monoid.PushoutI), HNN extensions, first-order syntax and computability. It plans effective free-group algorithms on reduced words (word, conjugacy, roots, centralizers), Stallings graphs of finitely generated subgroups, an effective first-order syntax for groups with basis coefficients, Bass–Serre theory with induced splittings and Grushko decompositions, equations, radicals and coordinate groups with equational Noetherianity of free groups, surface groups and quadratic equations, generalised equations with a terminating solver for equations and inequations over free groups and Merzljakov–Makanin formal solutions for positive sentences, fully residually free and limit groups with NTQ towers, Lyndon length functions and infinite words, effective JSJ decompositions and Makanin–Razborov diagrams, and the implicit function theorems for regular quadratic and regular NTQ systems. Every algorithm is planned as an encoded procedure with its interpretation, computability, termination on its stated input class and correctness of both answers. The full first-order decision procedure for free groups is outside the roadmap.

nodes.title: Primitive-recursive encoding of a free group through reduced words
nodes.statement: Let α be a type with DecidableEq α and Primcodable α. Equip FreeGroup α with the Primcodable structure transported along the injection toWord : FreeGroup α → List (α × Bool), whose range is the decidable set of reduced words: encode x is the code of toWord x, and decoding a code n returns mk L when n decodes to a list L with IsReduced L, and nothing otherwise. The carrier is Mathlib's FreeGroup α itself; no second free-group type is introduced.
hypotheses: α has decidable equality and a Primcodable structure (for a finite basis, α = Fin n or any Fintype with an explicit equivalence to Fin n).
proofSteps: The range of toWord is exactly the set of reduced words (Mathlib's isReduced_toWord, and reduce_toWord for the converse via IsReduced.reduce_eq).
IsReduced is a primitive recursive predicate on List (α × Bool): it is a chain condition checked by List recursion, using decidable equality of α and Bool; record this as the lemma primrec_isReduced.
Transport Primcodable along the subtype {L // IsReduced L} ≃ FreeGroup α given by toWord and mk (Mathlib's Primcodable.subtype for a primitive recursive predicate, then Primcodable.ofEquiv).
acceptance: encode (mk L) = encode (reduce L) for every word L.
Decoding the code of a non-reduced word, such as [(a,true),(a,false)], returns none.

nodes.title: Free reduction and the group operations are primitive recursive
nodes.statement: For Primcodable α with DecidableEq α: (1) FreeGroup.reduce : List (α × Bool) → List (α × Bool) is primitive recursive; (2) multiplication, inversion and natural and integer powers on FreeGroup α are primitive recursive for the encoding of FG1/primcodable-free-group; (3) the word length norm : FreeGroup α → ℕ is primitive recursive; (4) the interpretation theorems hold: toWord (x * y) = reduce (toWord x ++ toWord y), toWord x⁻¹ = invRev (toWord x), toWord (x ^ n) = reduce (n-fold concatenation of toWord x).
hypotheses: α is Primcodable with decidable equality.
proofSteps: reduce is defined by List recursion with a case split on the head of the recursively reduced tail; express it with Primrec.list_foldr (or list_rec) and the primitive recursive test that two letters cancel.

Multiplication is reduce applied to an append (Primrec.list_append); inversion is invRev, a list reverse composed with a letter map; powers iterate multiplication (Primrec.nat_iterate), and integer powers split on the sign.
The interpretation theorems are Mathlib's toWord_mul, toWord_inv and toWord_pow; norm is the length of toWord.
acceptance: Instantiating at α = Fin 2 gives a primitive recursive multiplication on F(a,b) whose value on (a b, b⁻¹ a) has reduced word [a, a].
The theorem is false for the naive concatenation of words, which is not an operation on FreeGroup α: the test is that toWord of the product is reduced.

nodes.title: Homomorphism evaluation and substitution are computable
nodes.statement: Let α be finite with DecidableEq α and Primcodable α. (1) For a group H with a Primcodable structure in which multiplication, inversion and the identity are primitive recursive, the evaluation map (α → H) × FreeGroup α → H, (f, w) ↦ lift f w, is primitive recursive, where α → H carries the Primcodable structure of finite functions. (2) In particular substitution FreeGroup α × (α → FreeGroup β) → FreeGroup β, (w, σ) ↦ w >>= σ, is primitive recursive for Primcodable β with DecidableEq β, and map f is primitive recursive for every function f : α → β.
hypotheses: α finite; H has primitive recursive group operations for its encoding.
proofSteps: Mathlib's lift_mk computes lift f (mk L) as the product of f a or its inverse along L; this is a list fold (Primrec.list_foldl) of primitive recursive operations.
Finite functions α → H are encoded as lists of values indexed by an enumeration of α; evaluation at a letter is list lookup.
Substitution is the case H = FreeGroup β using FG1/reduce-primrec for the group law of the target.
acceptance: For α = Fin 2, H = FreeGroup (Fin 2), σ(a) = a b, σ(b) = b: the substitution of [a,b] = a⁻¹ b⁻¹ a b returns the reduced word of b⁻¹ a⁻¹ b⁻¹ a b b, namely b⁻¹ a⁻¹ b⁻¹ a b².
Evaluation into a finite group given by its multiplication table (Fin m with primitive recursive table lookup) is an instance.

nodes.title: The word-problem procedure for a free group
nodes.statement: For α with DecidableEq α, define isTrivialWord : List (α × Bool) → Bool by isTrivialWord L = (reduce L).isEmpty, and the equality test eqWord L₁ L₂ = isTrivialWord (invRev L₁ ++ L₂). These are the encoded procedures for the word problem of FreeGroup α (inputs are arbitrary, possibly unreduced, words over the basis).
hypotheses: α has decidable equality.
proofSteps: Both procedures are compositions of reduce, invRev and append, total by structural recursion.
acceptance: isTrivialWord [(a,true),(b,true),(a,false),(b,false)] = false for a ≠ b (the commutator is nontrivial).
isTrivialWord [(a,true),(b,true),(b,false),(a,false)] = true.

nodes.title: Correctness of the word-problem procedure (both answers)
nodes.statement: For every word L, isTrivialWord L = true if and only if mk L = 1 in FreeGroup α; for all words L₁ L₂, eqWord L₁ L₂ = true if and only if mk L₁ = mk L₂. Hence a true answer certifies triviality and a false answer certifies nontriviality.
hypotheses: α has decidable equality.
proofSteps: mk L = 1 ↔ toWord (mk L) = [] (Mathlib's toWord_eq_nil_iff) and toWord (mk L) = reduce L (toWord_mk).
For eqWord use mk (invRev L₁ ++ L₂) = (mk L₁)⁻¹ * mk L₂ (inv_mk and mul_mk).

nodes.title: Conjugacy criterion: cyclic reductions agree up to cyclic permutation
nodes.statement: For x, y ∈ FreeGroup α, x and y are conjugate if and only if the cyclically reduced words reduceCyclically (toWord x) and reduceCyclically (toWord y) are cyclic permutations of each other (List.IsRotated). Moreover every element is conjugate, by the explicit word conjugator (toWord x), to the element of its cyclic reduction.
hypotheses: α has decidable equality.
proofSteps: By Mathlib's conj_conjugator_reduceCyclically, x is conjugate to the element u of its cyclic reduction; likewise y to v.
Rotating a cyclically reduced word is conjugation by a prefix, so rotated words give conjugate elements.

Conversely if g⁻¹ u g = v with u, v cyclically reduced, induct on the length of g: if |g| ≤ |u| then u = g ∘ u₁ and v = u₁ ∘ g, a rotation (the ℤ case of MRS-REGULAR Lemma 3.8(3)); if |g| > |u| then g = u^k g' after cancellation and u^k commutes with u, which reduces the length of the conjugator.
acceptance: a b and b a are conjugate in F(a,b); a b and a b⁻¹ are not (their cyclic reductions are not rotations of each other).
The criterion fails for words that are not cyclically reduced: a b a⁻¹ and b are conjugate though a b a⁻¹ is not a rotation of b, which is why the cyclic reduction is taken first.

nodes.title: The conjugacy procedure with witness
nodes.statement: Define conjWitness : List (α × Bool) → List (α × Bool) → Option (List (α × Bool)): reduce both inputs, cyclically reduce them recording the conjugators c₁, c₂ (FreeGroup.reduceCyclically.conjugator), then search the |u| rotations of the cyclic reduction u of the first input for one equal to the cyclic reduction v of the second; on success at rotation u = p ++ s, v = s ++ p, return the word c of the element c₁ · p · c₂⁻¹ (so that c⁻¹ · x · c = y with this convention), and return none if no rotation matches.
hypotheses: α has decidable equality.
proofSteps: The search is a bounded search over at most |u| + 1 rotations, so the procedure is total.
The conjugator returned is assembled from the recorded prefixes; its correctness is FG1/conjugacy-correct.

nodes.title: Maximal-root extraction
nodes.statement: Define maxRoot : FreeGroup α → FreeGroup α × ℕ as follows. If x = 1 return (1, 0). Otherwise write toWord x = c ++ u ++ invRev c with u = reduceCyclically (toWord x) nonempty and c its conjugator; let d be the least divisor of |u| such that u is the (|u|/d)-fold repetition of its prefix p of length d; return (mk (c ++ p ++ invRev c), |u|/d). The identity is handled explicitly: maxRoot 1 = (1, 0).
hypotheses: α has decidable equality.
proofSteps: The divisor search is bounded by |u|; checking that u is a repetition of a prefix is a list comparison.
Correctness (FG1/max-root-correct) uses that the power of a cyclically reduced word is the concatenation of copies (Mathlib's reduce_flatten_replicate).

nodes.title: Existence and uniqueness of maximal roots, and correctness of maxRoot
nodes.statement: For x ∈ FreeGroup α with x ≠ 1: (1) (r, k) := maxRoot x satisfies r ^ k = x, k ≥ 1 and r is not a proper power; (2) uniqueness: if s ^ m = x with m ≥ 1 and s not a proper power then s = r and m = k; (3) every root of x is a power of r: if y ^ n = x with n ≥ 1 then y = r ^ (k / n) and n ∣ k. For x = 1, maxRoot x = (1, 0).
proofSteps: Reduce to the cyclically reduced case by conjugation (FG1/conjugacy-criterion).

If s ^ m = x with s cyclically reduced then toWord x is the m-fold concatenation of toWord s (reduce_flatten_replicate); two primitive-period decompositions of the same word coincide by the Lyndon–Schützenberger periodicity argument (a word with two periods p, q with p + q ≤ length has period gcd(p, q)).
Root uniqueness for fixed exponent is Mathlib's torsion-freeness instance (pow_left_injective).
acceptance: For x = (a b)⁶: maxRoot x = (a b, 6), and the roots of x are (a b)^d for d ∣ 6.
The identity case is excluded from (1)–(3): 1 = 1² = 1³, so uniqueness of the exponent fails at 1.

nodes.title: Commuting elements of a free group are powers of a common element
nodes.statement: For x, y ∈ FreeGroup α: x * y = y * x if and only if there are r ∈ FreeGroup α and m, n ∈ ℤ with x = r ^ m and y = r ^ n. If x ≠ 1 one can take r = (maxRoot x).1.
proofSteps: If x = 1 take r = y. Otherwise conjugate so that x is cyclically reduced; y commutes with x, so y⁻¹ x y = x, and by FG1/conjugacy-criterion y conjugates the cyclically reduced word x to itself; induct on |y| as in that proof to get y ∈ ⟨maxRoot x⟩.
The converse is immediate.

nodes.title: Maximal cyclic subgroups are malnormal; free groups are CSA
nodes.statement: Let u ∈ FreeGroup α be nontrivial and not a proper power, and M = zpowers u. Then M is a maximal abelian subgroup and is malnormal: for g ∉ M, g M g⁻¹ ⊓ M = ⊥. Equivalently FreeGroup α is a CSA group (every maximal abelian subgroup is malnormal), and commutation is transitive on nontrivial elements.
proofSteps: Maximal abelian subgroups of F are trivial or the centralizers of nontrivial elements (FG1/centralizer-cyclic), i.e. zpowers of non-proper-powers.
If g u^m g⁻¹ = u^n with m, n ≠ 0, then m = n by comparing cyclic lengths (conjugate elements have equal cyclically reduced length) and g commutes with u^m, so g ∈ centralizer (u^m) = zpowers u.

nodes.title: Serre graphs: graphs with edge reversal, loops and multiple edges
nodes.statement: A Serre graph consists of a vertex type V, an edge type E, an origin map src : E → V and a reversal rev : E → E with rev (rev e) = e and rev e ≠ e for every edge; the terminus is tgt e := src (rev e). Loops (src e = tgt e) and multiple edges are allowed. An orientation is a subset E⁺ ⊆ E containing exactly one edge of each pair {e, rev e}. A path from u to w is a list of edges e₁ … e_k with src e₁ = u, tgt e_i = src e_{i+1} and tgt e_k = w (the empty path at u has u = w); a path is reduced when no e_{i+1} = rev e_i. The graph is connected when any two vertices are joined by a path, and is a tree when it is connected, nonempty and has no reduced closed path of positive length.
proofSteps: Structure with the four fields and two axioms; paths as lists with a chain condition; reduced paths by a second chain condition.
acceptance: The one-vertex graph with one pair of loop edges {e, ē} (the rose with one petal) is connected and not a tree.

nodes.title: Maximal trees exist and the fundamental group of a graph is free
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a connected Serre graph and v a vertex. (1) Γ has a maximal subtree T containing every vertex; for finite Γ, T is computed by breadth-first search. (2) The set π₁(Γ, v) of reduced closed paths at v, with concatenation followed by reduction, is a group, free with basis indexed by the positive edges of Γ outside T: the basis element for e is the reduced loop (path in T from v to src e) · e · (path in T from tgt e to v). (3) For finite Γ, rank π₁(Γ, v) = #E⁺ − #V + 1.
hypotheses: Γ connected (for (2), (3)); for (3), Γ finite.
proofSteps: (1) Zorn's lemma on subtrees for general Γ (Serre I.2.3, Proposition 11); for finite Γ a search tree.
(2) Every reduced closed path factors uniquely as a reduced product of the T-loops of the edges it crosses outside T.
(3) A finite tree has #E⁺ = #V − 1 (KM02 Lemma 8.2 counts #E⁺(Γ − T)).
acceptance: For the rose with n petals, T is the vertex and π₁ is free of rank n.
For the theta graph (two vertices, three edges) the rank is 3 − 2 + 1 = 2.

nodes.title: α-labelled graphs (X-digraphs) and the subgroup they accept
nodes.statement: For a type α, an α-labelled graph is a Serre graph Γ with a labelling μ : E → α × Bool such that μ (rev e) = (a, !b) when μ e = (a, b). The label of a path is the word of its edge labels, an element of List (α × Bool). For a vertex v, the subgroup accepted at v is subgroup Γ v := {mk (label p) | p a closed path at v} ≤ FreeGroup α; it equals the set of freely reduced labels of reduced closed paths when Γ is folded. A morphism of labelled graphs is a Serre-graph morphism preserving labels; a based graph (Γ, v) is a labelled graph with a base vertex. A labelled graph is folded when no vertex is the origin of two distinct edges with the same label, and it is a core graph at v when every vertex and edge lies on a reduced closed path at v.
proofSteps: Structure extending SerreGraph with the labelling and its equivariance axiom; subgroup Γ v is the image of the label map on closed paths, which is closed under products (concatenation) and inverses (reversal).
acceptance: The rose with petals labelled a, b accepts F(a,b) at its vertex.
A single edge labelled a from v to w ≠ v accepts the trivial subgroup at v.

nodes.title: Stallings correspondence: subgroups and based folded core graphs
nodes.statement: Let α be finite. (1) For every subgroup H ≤ FreeGroup α there is a connected folded based graph (Γ(H), 1_H), a core graph at 1_H, with subgroup Γ(H) 1_H = H; it is unique up to a unique based isomorphism. (2) Γ(H) is finite if and only if H is finitely generated, and then Γ(H) ≅ stallingsGraph ws for any finite generating list ws. (3) For subgroups K, H: K ≤ H if and only if there is a based morphism Γ(K) → Γ(H), which is then unique. (4) Forgetting base points: the core of Γ(H) at any vertex (the unbased core, obtained by also removing the hanging path to 1_H) determines H up to conjugacy.
hypotheses: α finite (the basis of F is finite); H any subgroup for (1), finitely generated for the finiteness clause of (2).
proofSteps: (1) Existence from the coset graph H\F with its core (KM02 Theorem 5.1); uniqueness from uniqueness of morphisms between folded graphs (Lemma 4.2) and the existence of morphisms for containments (Proposition 4.3) (KM02 Theorem 5.2).
(2) KM02 Lemma 5.4 with Proposition 3.8.
(3) KM02 Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.3.
(4) KM02 §7, Proposition 7.7 (subgroups are conjugate iff their unbased cores are isomorphic as labelled graphs).

nodes.statement: For finite lists of words: (1) memberTest ws w reads the reduced word of w from the base vertex of stallingsGraph ws and answers true exactly when the reading succeeds and ends at the base vertex; (2) interGens ws us builds the product graph of stallingsGraph ws and stallingsGraph us (vertex pairs, an edge with label x between pairs joined by x-edges in both factors), takes its core at the pair of base vertices and returns the basis words of FG2/nielsen-basis; (3) indexOf ws returns some (number of vertices) when stallingsGraph ws is complete (every vertex has an outgoing edge with every label in α × Bool) and none otherwise; (4) conjSubgroupWitness ws us returns a word g with g⁻¹ ⟨ws⟩ g = ⟨us⟩ when the unbased cores of the two Stallings graphs are isomorphic as labelled graphs (searching the finitely many label-preserving bijections and base-point paths) and none otherwise; (5) conjContainWitness ws us returns g with g⁻¹ ⟨us⟩ g ≤ ⟨ws⟩ when there is a morphism from the unbased core of Γ(⟨us⟩) to Γ(⟨ws⟩), and none otherwise.

nodes.title: Intersections: product graphs and the Howson property
nodes.statement: For subgroups H, K ≤ FreeGroup α and vertices v of Γ(H), w of Γ(K): the core at (v, w) of the product graph Γ(H) × Γ(K) is the subgroup graph of H ∩ K. Consequently (Howson) the intersection of two finitely generated subgroups of a free group is finitely generated, and interGens computes a free basis of it: Subgroup.closure (interGens ws us) = ⟨ws⟩ ⊓ ⟨us⟩.
proofSteps: The product of folded graphs is folded (KM02 Lemma 9.2) and a closed path at (v, w) projects to closed paths in both factors; conversely two closed paths with the same reduced label combine (KM02 Proposition 9.4).

nodes.title: Finite index, the index algorithm and the Schreier formula
nodes.statement: Let α be finite and H ≤ FreeGroup α. (1) H has finite index if and only if Γ(H) is finite and complete (every vertex has an outgoing edge with each label in α × Bool), and then H.index = #V(Γ(H)); hence indexOf ws = some n iff ⟨ws⟩.index = n ≠ 0. (2) (Schreier formula, exact form) If H has finite index i then H is finitely generated and Group.rank H − 1 = i · (|α| − 1).

proofSteps: (1) KM02 Proposition 8.3: coset representatives are the labels of tree paths to the vertices.
(2) KM02 Corollary 8.4: in a complete graph #E⁺ = |α| · #V, and rank H − 1 = #E⁺ − #V by FG2/nielsen-basis. Mathlib's Subgroup.rank_le_index_mul_rank gives only an inequality.

nodes.title: The language of groups and its coefficient extensions
nodes.statement: Language.group is the first-order language with one constant symbol one, one unary function symbol inv and one binary function symbol mul, and no relation symbols. Every group G is a Language.group-structure by interpreting the symbols as 1, x ↦ x⁻¹ and multiplication. For a type A of coefficient names, L_A := Language.group[[A]] adds a constant for each a ∈ A; a group G together with c : A → G is an L_A-structure. For a coefficient group generated by A (in particular F(A) with c = of), the sentences of L_A over (G, c) are the sentences of the source's language L_A. The theory of groups is the set of the three group axioms as L-sentences.
proofSteps: Define the language by its function-symbol family indexed by arity (0, 1, 2) and the empty relation family.
Instances: Group G gives Language.group.Structure G; a map c : A → G gives the constants structure, hence an L_A-structure (Mathlib's constantsOn structure for withConstants).
acceptance: Every group is a model of the theory of groups; a monoid that is not a group (ℕ under addition, with inv interpreted arbitrarily) is not.
With A = Fin 2 and c = of : Fin 2 → F(a,b), the atomic L_A-sentence mul(a, b) = mul(b, a) is false in F(a,b) and true in ℤ² with c(0) = (1,0), c(1) = (0,1).

hypotheses: Free-variable tables are finite; prenex semantics uses a nonempty structure (automatic for groups).
proofSteps: Each operation is defined by structural recursion on terms or formulas; on codes it is a list transformation with bounded recursion.
Capture is impossible: bound variables are de Bruijn indices in Mathlib's BoundedFormula, and liftAt performs the shift that substitution under a binder needs.
Semantic correctness is Mathlib's realize_subst, realize_relabel and realize_toPrenex.
acceptance: Substituting mul(y, a) for x in ∃z (mul(x, z) = one) yields ∃z (mul(mul(y,a), z) = one) without capturing z.

An atomic formula t = s corresponds to the word equation toWord t * (toWord s)⁻¹ = 1.
proofSteps: Structural recursion on terms; ofWord by recursion on toWord of the element.

nodes.title: Finite systems of equations and inequations with word coefficients
nodes.statement: For finite types X (variables) and A (basis of the coefficient free group), an equation–inequation system is a pair (S, T) of finite lists of words in FreeGroup (X ⊕ A). An assignment v : X → G into a group G with coefficients c : A → G solves (S, T) when FreeGroup.lift (Sum.elim v c) s = 1 for every s ∈ S and FreeGroup.lift (Sum.elim v c) t ≠ 1 for every t ∈ T. Solutions in FreeGroup A use c = of.
proofSteps: A structure with two lists and a solution predicate.
acceptance: The system ([x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹], [x]) over F(a,b) has the solution x = a, y = a².
The system ([x a x⁻¹ a⁻¹, x b x⁻¹ b⁻¹], [x]) has no solution in F(a,b): an element commuting with a and b is trivial.

nodes.title: Quantifier-free formulas are finite disjunctions of systems
nodes.statement: There is a primitive recursive function toSystems sending a quantifier-free L_A-formula φ with free variables in X to a finite list of equation–inequation systems (S_i, T_i) over FreeGroup (X ⊕ A) such that, in every group G with coefficients c : A → G and every v : X → G, φ is realized by (v, c) if and only if v solves (S_i, T_i) for some i.
hypotheses: φ is quantifier-free (Mathlib's IsQF).
proofSteps: Push negations to atoms and distribute conjunction over disjunction (disjunctive normal form, by recursion on IsQF using Mathlib's IsQF.induction_on_sup_not).
Replace each atom t = s by the word toWord t * (toWord s)⁻¹ (FG3/term-to-word), positive atoms into S_i and negated atoms into T_i.
Correctness by induction using realize_equal_iff; computability by FG3/syntax-operations-computable and the primitive recursiveness of toWord.
acceptance: φ = ¬(x = a) ∨ (x y = y x) gives the two systems ([], [x a⁻¹]) and ([x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹], []).
In a nontrivial group the source's further normalisation (each disjunct with exactly one equation and one inequation) is not used: inequations are kept as a list.

nodes.title: Existential and universal sentences reduce to systems
nodes.statement: There are primitive recursive functions existsToSystems and forallToSystems on codes of L_A-sentences such that: (1) if σ is an existential sentence ∃x₁…∃x_k φ with φ quantifier-free (Mathlib's IsExistential, normalised by toPrenex), then G ⊨ σ (with coefficients c) iff some system in existsToSystems σ has a solution in G; (2) if σ is universal, then G ⊨ σ iff no system in forallToSystems σ (the systems of the negated matrix) has a solution in G. The reduction is uniform in G: it uses only the group axioms.
hypotheses: σ existential (respectively universal) in Mathlib's sense; G any group with coefficients.
proofSteps: Strip the existential block to obtain φ with free variables Fin k and apply FG3/quantifier-free-normal-form.
For universal sentences, negate: ∀x φ holds iff ∃x ¬φ fails, and ¬φ is quantifier-free.
Computability from FG3/syntax-operations-computable.
acceptance: σ = ∃x (x a = a x ∧ x ≠ 1) reduces to the single system ([x a x⁻¹ a⁻¹], [x]), solvable in F(a,b) (x = a).
σ = ∀x ∀y (x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹ = 1) holds in ℤ² and fails in F(a,b): the negated system ([], [x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹]) is solvable exactly in nonabelian groups.

nodes.title: Graphs of groups
nodes.statement: A graph of groups 𝔸 over a Serre graph A (FG2/serre-graph) assigns a group A_v to each vertex, a group A_e to each edge with A_{rev e} = A_e, and for each edge an injective homomorphism ω_e : A_e →* A_{tgt e}, with α_e := ω_{rev e} : A_e →* A_{src e}. Loops and multiple edges are allowed; no finiteness is assumed in the definition, and ‘finite graph of groups’ means a finite underlying graph.
proofSteps: Structure over a Serre graph with dependent families of groups and monomorphisms satisfying the reversal compatibility.
acceptance: The segment with vertex groups ℤ, ℤ and edge group ℤ mapped by 2 and 3 is a graph of groups (π₁ is the torus-knot-type group ⟨x, y | x² = y³⟩).
A one-vertex graph with one loop pair, A_v = A_e = ℤ, α_e = id, ω_e = ×2, is a graph of groups (π₁ ≅ BS(1,2)).

nodes.title: The fundamental group of a graph of groups, via paths and via a maximal tree
nodes.statement: For a graph of groups 𝔸 and a vertex v₀: (1) an 𝔸-path from v to v′ is a sequence a₀, e₁, a₁, …, e_k, a_k with e₁…e_k an edge path from v to v′, a₀ ∈ A_v, a_k ∈ A_{v′}, a_i ∈ A_{tgt e_i} = A_{src e_{i+1}}; π₁(𝔸, v₀) is the set of 𝔸-paths from v₀ to v₀ modulo the equivalence generated by a, e, ω_e(c), rev e, a′ ∼ a α_e(c) a′, with concatenation as product. (2) For a maximal tree T of A, π₁(𝔸, T) is the quotient of the free product of the A_v (Monoid.CoprodI) and the free group on E by the relations rev e = e⁻¹, e ω_e(c) e⁻¹ = α_e(c) (convention fixed here, matching (1)), and e = 1 for e ∈ T. There is a canonical isomorphism π₁(𝔸, v₀) ≃* π₁(𝔸, T) sending the loop [v₀, src e]_T e [tgt e, v₀]_T to e.
hypotheses: A connected (for (2) and the isomorphism).
proofSteps: (1) Define 𝔸-paths and elementary equivalences; concatenation descends to the quotient (FOLD Definition 2.3).
(2) Define the presentation as a quotient of Monoid.Coprod (Monoid.CoprodI A_·) (FreeGroup E) by a normal closure.
The isomorphism sends a generator to the corresponding T-loop; its inverse reads an 𝔸-path letter by letter (FOLD Proposition 2.4(3) gives the generating set).
acceptance: For the segment, π₁(𝔸, T) is the amalgam A ∗_C B.
Changing the maximal tree gives isomorphic groups (FG4/maximal-tree-independence).

nodes.title: Normal form theorem and injectivity of vertex groups
nodes.statement: Let 𝔸 be a graph of groups. (1) A nontrivial element a ∈ A_v, as a length-zero path, is not equivalent to the trivial path; hence each vertexHom A_v →* π₁(𝔸, v₀) is injective. (2) A reduced 𝔸-path (one containing no subsequence a, e, ω_e(c), rev e, a′) of positive length is not equivalent to a shorter path, and two equivalent reduced 𝔸-paths have the same underlying edge path. (3) In particular, for the segment, Mathlib's normal form for Monoid.PushoutI is recovered, and for the loop Mathlib's normal form for HNNExtension (Britton's lemma: a word t^{ε₁} g₁ … with no pinch t c t⁻¹, c ∈ A, or t⁻¹ c t, c ∈ B, is nontrivial).
proofSteps: Construct an action of π₁(𝔸, v₀) on the set of reduced normal-form words relative to transversals of the edge-group images, as Mathlib does for PushoutI and HNNExtension, and check the relations (FOLD Proposition 2.4, Serre I §5.2 Theorem 11).
(1) and (2) follow because the action sends the empty word to the normal form of the path.
acceptance: In ⟨a, t | t a² t⁻¹ = a⟩ the path t a t⁻¹ is reduced because a ∉ ω(ℤ) = ⟨a²⟩, so t a t⁻¹ ∉ ⟨a⟩; the path t a² t⁻¹ is not reduced and equals a.
For the segment with C → A, C → B the identity maps of a common group, π₁ = A and a reduced path of positive length does not exist.

nodes.title: Group actions on trees: elliptic and hyperbolic elements, relative trees
nodes.statement: A G-tree is a Serre tree T with an action of G by graph automorphisms without inversions (g · e ≠ rev e for all g, e). An element g is elliptic when it fixes a vertex and hyperbolic otherwise; a subgroup H is elliptic when it fixes a vertex. For a family 𝒜 of subgroups closed under conjugation and taking subgroups and a family ℋ of subgroups, an (𝒜, ℋ)-tree is a G-tree whose edge stabilizers lie in 𝒜 and in which every H ∈ ℋ is elliptic. T is minimal when it has no proper G-invariant subtree. T dominates T′ when there is a G-equivariant map T → T′, equivalently when every vertex stabilizer of T is elliptic in T′; two trees are in the same deformation space when each dominates the other.
proofSteps: Define the action structure, the predicates elliptic, hyperbolic, minimal, the relative-tree predicate and domination.
acceptance: F(a,b) acting on its Cayley tree: every nontrivial element is hyperbolic.
In the Bass–Serre tree of A ∗_C B, A and B are elliptic and a b (a ∈ A ∖ C, b ∈ B ∖ C) is hyperbolic.

nodes.title: The Bass–Serre tree of a graph of groups
nodes.statement: For a graph of groups 𝔸 with base vertex v₀, the Bass–Serre tree X(𝔸, v₀) has as vertices the classes p A_v of 𝔸-paths p from v₀ to v (p ≈ p′ when p ∼ p′ a with a ∈ A_v), with an edge between p A_v and p a e A_{v′} for a ∈ A_v and an edge e from v to v′. π₁(𝔸, v₀) acts by left concatenation, without inversions. X is a tree; the stabilizer of p A_v is p A_v p⁻¹ and the stabilizer of the edge from p A_v to p a e A_{v′} is p a α_e(A_e) a⁻¹ p⁻¹; the quotient graph is A.
proofSteps: Define the vertex and edge sets as quotients of 𝔸-paths and the action by concatenation (FOLD Definition 2.5).
Connectedness by induction on path length; absence of reduced circuits from FG4/normal-form-theorem (2).
acceptance: For F(a,b) = ℤ ∗ ℤ with the segment of trivial edge group, X is the tree whose vertices are cosets of ⟨a⟩ and ⟨b⟩, bipartite with all vertices of infinite degree.

nodes.title: Structure theorem: actions on trees are graphs of groups
nodes.statement: Let a group U act on a tree Y without inversions. Then the quotient graph B = Y/U carries a graph of groups 𝔹 (vertex groups stabilizers of lifts of vertices along a lift T₁ of a maximal tree and a fundamental domain T₂, edge groups edge stabilizers, monomorphisms inclusions twisted by chosen elements t_v) such that U ≃* π₁(𝔹, v₀′) and Y is U-equivariantly isomorphic to the Bass–Serre tree of 𝔹. The resulting graph of groups is independent of the choices up to isomorphism of graphs of groups.
proofSteps: Choose T₁ ⊆ T₂ ⊆ Y as in FOLD Remark 2.7 and define 𝔹.

The map π₁(𝔹, T) → U is surjective since U is generated by the vertex stabilizers along T₁ and the t_v; injectivity and the tree isomorphism come from comparing Y with the Bass–Serre tree (Serre I §5.4 Theorem 13).

nodes.title: Elliptic–hyperbolic dichotomy and fixed points of finitely generated groups
nodes.statement: Let G act on a tree T without inversions. (1) Every g ∈ G is either elliptic or hyperbolic; a hyperbolic g has a unique axis, a g-invariant bi-infinite line on which it translates by ℓ(g) > 0. (2) If H ≤ G is finitely generated and every element of H is elliptic, then H fixes a vertex (for a finite generating set, it suffices that every generator and every product of two generators is elliptic). (3) If H contains a hyperbolic element then T contains a unique minimal H-invariant subtree μ_T(H), the union of the axes of hyperbolic elements of H.
hypotheses: Action without inversions; H finitely generated in (2).
proofSteps: (1) Serre I §6.4, Propositions 24–25: consider the minimum of d(x, g x).
(2) Serre I §6.5, Corollary 2 (Serre's lemma on pairs of elliptic elements); GL-JSJ Proposition 1.1 shows the third alternative (fixing an end) only occurs for infinitely generated H.
(3) GL-JSJ Proposition 1.1(2).
acceptance: In F(a,b) on its Cayley tree, a and b are hyperbolic, with axes meeting in one vertex.
ℚ (infinitely generated) can act on a tree with all elements elliptic and no global fixed point, so the finite-generation hypothesis in (2) is needed.

nodes.title: Induced splittings of subgroups, with finiteness under finite generation
nodes.statement: Let G = π₁(𝔸, v₀) with Bass–Serre tree X and base vertex x₀, and let U ≤ G. For a U-invariant subtree Y ⊆ X containing x₀, the induced splitting of U is the graph of groups of the structure theorem for the action of U on Y; its vertex groups are U ∩ conjugates of vertex groups of 𝔸 and its edge groups U ∩ conjugates of edge groups. The preferred subtree is X_{U,x₀} := ⋃_{u ∈ U} [x₀, u x₀]. If U is generated by a finite set S, then X_{U,x₀} = U · ⋃_{s ∈ S} [x₀, s x₀], so the induced graph of groups on X_{U,x₀}/U is finite; without finite generation it may be infinite.
hypotheses: For finiteness: U finitely generated.
proofSteps: Apply FG4/structure-theorem to the action of U on Y.
For finite S: the union of the geodesics [x₀, s x₀] meets every U-orbit of edges of X_{U,x₀}, because [x₀, s₁⋯s_k x₀] ⊆ ⋃ s₁⋯s_{i−1}[x₀, s_i x₀].
acceptance: For U = ⟨a b⟩ ≤ ℤ ∗ ℤ = ⟨a⟩ ∗ ⟨b⟩, the induced splitting is a loop with trivial groups (U ≅ ℤ acts freely on its axis).

nodes.title: Kurosh subgroup theorem, Grushko–Neumann theorem and Grushko decompositions
nodes.statement: (1) (Kurosh) Every subgroup U of a free product ∗_i G_i is a free product of a free group and of subgroups U ∩ g G_i g⁻¹ (one for each double coset U g G_i with nontrivial intersection). (2) (Grushko–Neumann) For finitely generated nontrivial G₁, G₂, rank (G₁ ∗ G₂) = rank G₁ + rank G₂. (3) (Grushko decomposition) Every finitely generated group G is a free product G = G₁ ∗ ⋯ ∗ G_p ∗ F_q with each G_i nontrivial, not ℤ and freely indecomposable; p, q are unique and the G_i are unique up to conjugacy and permutation. (4) (Relative version) For a finite family ℋ of finitely generated subgroups, the same holds for free decompositions in which every H ∈ ℋ is conjugate into some factor, with the G_i freely indecomposable relative to the conjugates of ℋ they contain; the trees of these decompositions form one deformation space (the Grushko deformation space relative to ℋ).
hypotheses: (2)–(4): finitely generated groups; (4): ℋ finite family of finitely generated subgroups.
proofSteps: (1) Apply FG4/induced-splitting to U acting on the tree of the free product (trivial edge stabilizers).
(2) Folding argument on 𝔸-graphs with the complexity of FOLD Definition 6.1 (FOLD Theorem 6.2).
(3) Existence by induction on rank using (2); uniqueness by (1) applied to two decompositions (the factors of one are elliptic in the tree of the other).
(4) The same argument for (trivial edge group, ℋ)-trees; GL-JSJ §3.2 identifies the Grushko deformation space.
acceptance: rank(ℤ/2 ∗ ℤ/3) = 2; rank(F₂ ∗ ℤ) = 3.
The Grushko decomposition of ℤ² ∗ F₂ has p = 1, q = 2, G₁ = ℤ².

nodes.title: Collapses, refinements and domination of splittings
nodes.statement: For a G-tree T and a G-invariant set of edges E′, the collapse T/E′ (contract each edge of E′) is a G-tree dominated by T, with vertex stabilizers generated by stabilizers of the collapsed subtrees; every G-equivariant map T → T′ factors through a collapse followed by folds. If T₁ is elliptic with respect to T₂ (every edge stabilizer of T₁ is elliptic in T₂), there is a refinement T̂₁ of T₁ dominating T₂ (the standard refinement) with collapse maps T̂₁ → T₁. Moves that preserve the set of elliptic subgroups (collapses of edges e with G_e = G_{src e}, their inverse expansions, and slides) preserve the deformation space.
proofSteps: Collapses: quotient of a tree by a G-invariant forest is a tree; the induced map is equivariant.
Standard refinement: blow up each vertex v of T₁ into a G_v-invariant subtree of T₂ (GL-JSJ Proposition 2.2).
Deformation-space moves: GL-JSJ Remark 2.13 and the references there.
acceptance: Collapsing the edge of A ∗_C B gives the trivial tree, dominated by every tree.

nodes.title: Dehn twists of one-edge splittings
nodes.statement: (1) For G = A ∗_C B (Mathlib's Monoid.PushoutI over Bool) and z ∈ Subgroup.centralizer C with z ∈ B (or z ∈ A), the Dehn twist τ_z is the automorphism with τ_z(a) = a for a ∈ A and τ_z(b) = z b z⁻¹ for b ∈ B (well defined since z centralizes C). (2) For G = HNNExtension A C₁ C₂ φ (Mathlib’s convention t a t⁻¹ = φ(a) for a ∈ C₁) and z ∈ A centralizing C₁, τ_z is the automorphism fixing A pointwise and sending t to t z; it is well defined because (t z) a (t z)⁻¹ = t a t⁻¹ = φ(a) for a ∈ C₁. (3) τ_z fixes the vertex group containing the base pointwise, acts on the other vertex group by conjugation, fixes the edge group pointwise, preserves the conjugacy class of every subgroup elliptic in the splitting, and τ_z τ_w = τ_{zw} for z, w in the same centralizer.
hypotheses: z centralizes the edge group (inside the vertex group indicated).
proofSteps: Define τ_z by the universal property (Monoid.PushoutI.lift, HNNExtension.lift), check the relations using that z centralizes the amalgamated subgroup, and invert by τ_{z⁻¹}.
acceptance: For F(a,b) = ⟨a⟩ ∗ ⟨b⟩ (C trivial) and z = b, τ_b fixes a and b: twisting a free splitting by an element of the factor B is inner on B and the identity on A.

nodes.statement: Let H be a G-group and S ⊆ G[X]. The algebraic set V_H(S) ⊆ (X → H) is {v | ∀ s ∈ S, s(v) = 1}. For Y ⊆ (X → H), the ideal I_H(Y) = {w ∈ G[X] | ∀ v ∈ Y, w(v) = 1} is a normal subgroup. nodes.title: Noetherian Zariski topology and irreducible components
nodes.statement: Let H be G-equationally Noetherian. (1) For every finite X the Zariski topology on X → H is Noetherian (descending chain condition on closed sets), and conversely Noetherianity for all n implies G-equational Noetherianity. (2) Every closed set Y is a finite union Y = Y₁ ∪ … ∪ Y_m of irreducible closed sets with Y_i ⊄ Y_j for i ≠ j, and this irredundant decomposition is unique up to order (the Y_i are the maximal irreducible closed subsets). (3) The coordinate group Γ(Y) embeds canonically in Γ(Y₁) × … × Γ(Y_m).
hypotheses: H G-equationally Noetherian (no domain hypothesis is needed for (1)–(3)).
proofSteps: (1) ALG Proposition 10 and Theorem D1: chains of algebraic sets stabilise.
(2) Mathlib's NoetherianSpace gives finitely many irreducible components (ALG Corollary 11).
(3) ALG Proposition 12: I(Y) = ⋂ I(Y_i).
acceptance: Over F(a,b), V({[[x,a],[x,b]^g] : g}) = ⟨a⟩ ∪ ⟨b⟩ has the two components ⟨a⟩ and ⟨b⟩, and Γ embeds in Γ(⟨a⟩) × Γ(⟨b⟩).

sources.locator: §3.6, Proposition 10, p. 37; Theorem D1 (introduction p. 9, proof §3.6, p. 38); Corollaries 10–11 and Proposition 12, p. 39
sources.match: Equational Noetherianity is the descending chain condition on algebraic sets; closed sets are finite unions of uniquely determined irreducible components; the coordinate group embeds in the product of those of the components.

nodes.title: Irreducibility is discrimination of the coordinate group
nodes.statement: Let H be a G-equationally Noetherian G-domain and Y ⊆ (X → H) closed. Then Y is irreducible if and only if Γ(Y) is G-discriminated by H. Every coordinate group Γ(Y) is G-separated by H, and for any S, Rad_H(S) = ncl(S) if and only if G_S is G-separated by H. In particular, for a reducible Y, Γ(Y) is G-separated but not G-discriminated by H: a radical quotient need not be fully residually H.
hypotheses: H a G-equationally Noetherian G-domain (for the irreducibility criterion).
proofSteps: Separation: I(Y) is the intersection of the kernels of the evaluations at points of Y (ALG Corollary 8); the same argument gives the criterion for Rad = ncl.

Irreducible ⇒ discriminated: for finitely many nontrivial elements, each is nonzero on a proper closed subset's complement, and irreducibility makes the intersection of the nonempty open sets nonempty (ALG Lemma 15).
Discriminated ⇒ irreducible: if Y = Y₁ ∪ Y₂ properly, pick w_i ∈ I(Y_i) ∖ I(Y); a G-homomorphism nonzero on both w₁, w₂ is a point of Y outside Y₁ ∪ Y₂ (ALG Theorem 5).
acceptance: Γ(⟨a⟩ ∪ ⟨b⟩) over F(a,b) is F-separated but not F-discriminated by F.
Γ(V([x, a])) = F ∗_{⟨a⟩} ⟨a, t | [a,t]⟩ is F-discriminated by F (an extension of a centralizer).

nodes.title: Points as homomorphisms; word maps and changes of coordinates
nodes.statement: Let H be a G-group. (1) For an algebraic set Y ⊆ (X → H), evaluation gives a bijection Hom_G(Γ(Y), H) ≃ Y. (2) Word maps (morphisms of algebraic sets given by tuples of elements of G[X]) correspond contravariantly to G-homomorphisms of coordinate groups, giving an equivalence (anti-equivalence) between algebraic sets over H with word maps and their coordinate groups with G-homomorphisms. (3) A G-automorphism σ of G[X] (a change of coordinates) maps V_H(S) bijectively onto V_H(σ⁻¹(S)) and induces G_{R(S)} ≅ G_{R(σ⁻¹ S)}.
proofSteps: (1) A G-homomorphism Γ(Y) → H is determined by the images of X, which form a point of V(I(Y)) = Y.
(2) ALG Theorem 4 and Corollary 9.
(3) Specialisation of (2) to invertible word maps.

nodes.title: Surface groups with boundary and their peripheral structure
nodes.statement: For g, m ∈ ℕ: the orientable surface group S⁺(g, m) is PresentedGroup on generators a₁, b₁, …, a_g, b_g, p₁, …, p_m with the single relator [a₁,b₁] ⋯ [a_g,b_g] p₁ ⋯ p_m (commutator convention [x, y] = x⁻¹ y⁻¹ x y), and the non-orientable surface group S⁻(g, m), g ≥ 1, has generators c₁, …, c_g, p₁, …, p_m and relator c₁² ⋯ c_g² p₁ ⋯ p_m. The peripheral (boundary) elements are p₁, …, p_m, and the boundary subgroups are their cyclic subgroups and conjugates. The Euler characteristic is χ = 2 − 2g − m (orientable) or χ = 2 − g − m (non-orientable). Closed surface groups are the case m = 0.

nodes.title: Surface groups with boundary are free; closed ones are not
nodes.statement: (1) For m ≥ 1, S±(g, m) is free of rank 1 − χ, with free basis a₁, b₁, …, a_g, b_g, p₁, …, p_{m−1} (respectively c₁, …, c_g, p₁, …, p_{m−1}); p_m is the inverse of the product of the others in the relator order. (2) For m = 0 and χ ≤ 0, S±(g, 0) is not free: for the orientable case, a free group of rank 2g with this abelianisation would make the defining surjection FreeGroup (Fin 2g) → S⁺(g, 0) an isomorphism (free groups of finite rank are Hopfian), contradicting the nontriviality of the relator; for the non-orientable case the abelianisation has torsion. (3) Closed surface groups with χ ≤ 0 are torsion-free.
proofSteps: (1) Eliminate p_m using the relator (a Tietze move), leaving no relator.

(2) Free groups of finite rank are Hopfian: they are residually finite (embed in SL(2, ℤ) by FG5/free-group-linear and reduce modulo large integers; the current Tau Ceti library also proves it as FreeGroup.instResiduallyFinite) and finitely generated residually finite groups are Hopfian (Malcev's argument with the finitely many homomorphisms to each finite group); the relator is nontrivial by FG1/word-problem-correct.
(3) From the graph-of-groups splitting FG6/surface-splittings with free vertex groups and torsion-free edge groups.

nodes.title: Cutting and gluing: surface groups as graphs of groups
nodes.statement: (1) Gluing: for g = g₁ + g₂, S⁺(g, m₁ + m₂) is the amalgam S⁺(g₁, m₁ + 1) ∗_{ℤ} S⁺(g₂, m₂ + 1) along the last boundary elements (with inverse orientation), and S⁺(g, m) is the HNN extension of S⁺(g − 1, m + 2) identifying two boundary elements (a non-separating curve); the analogous statements hold for non-orientable surfaces with the standard curves. nodes.title: Finite-index subgroups of surface groups and the Euler characteristic
nodes.statement: Let Σ = S±(g, m) and H ≤ Σ of finite index n. Then H, with the induced peripheral structure (the subgroups H ∩ x⟨p_j⟩x⁻¹, one H-conjugacy class for each double coset H x ⟨p_j⟩), is isomorphic to a surface group S±(g′, m′) with its peripheral structure, where χ′ = n · χ, m′ is the number of such double cosets, and the orientability type is orientable when Σ is orientable. For m ≥ 1 this refines the Schreier formula: rank H − 1 = n (rank Σ − 1).
hypotheses: [Σ : H] = n finite.
proofSteps: Build the finite cover of the presentation 2-complex of Σ (one vertex, the generators as edges, one polygon) corresponding to H; each edge lies on exactly two polygon sides and vertex links are circles or arcs, so the cover is a combinatorial surface with n polygons.

Bring its polygon gluing to one polygon with a standard boundary word by the moves of FG6/quadratic-standard-form (cut-and-paste moves are changes of generators); this gives the standard presentation of H and the boundary count.
χ is the alternating count of cells, multiplied by n under the cover; for m ≥ 1 compare with FG2/finite-index-schreier.

nodes.title: Quadratic words, standard quadratic equations and their solutions
nodes.statement: Let G be a group and S ⊆ G[X]. S is quadratic when every variable occurring in S occurs at most twice (as x or x⁻¹) in the reduced forms of the elements of S, and strictly quadratic when exactly twice. A standard quadratic equation over G is one of: (1) ∏_{i=1}^{n} [x_i, y_i] = 1, n > 0; (2) ∏_{i=1}^{n} [x_i, y_i] ∏_{j=1}^{m} z_j⁻¹ c_j z_j d = 1, n, m ≥ 0, n + m ≥ 1; (3) ∏_{i=1}^{n} x_i² = 1, n > 0; (4) ∏_{i=1}^{n} x_i² ∏_{j=1}^{m} z_j⁻¹ c_j z_j d = 1, n, m ≥ 0, n + m ≥ 1, with d, c_j nontrivial elements of G; types (1)–(2) are orientable and (3)–(4) non-orientable of genus n. Atoms are [x, y], x², z⁻¹ c z; the atomic rank r(S) is the number of atoms. A solution φ of a standard equation written r₁ ⋯ r_k d = 1 (k ≥ 2) is degenerate if some r_i^φ = 1, commutative if [r_i^φ, r_{i+1}^φ] = 1 for all i, and in general position if [r_i^φ, r_{i+1}^φ] ≠ 1 for all i. S is consistent when it has a solution in G.
proofSteps: Predicates on elements of G[X] (occurrence counts in the reduced form of Monoid.Coprod words) and an inductive description of the four standard shapes.
acceptance: x² y² z² = 1 is standard of type (3), genus 3, r(S) = 3.
x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹ x = 1 is not quadratic (x occurs three times).

nodes.title: Effective reduction of quadratic words to standard form
nodes.statement: For every strictly quadratic word W ∈ G[X] there is a G-automorphism f of G[X] (a change of coordinates, FG5/points-and-coordinate-changes) such that f(W) is a standard quadratic word (up to cyclic permutation and conjugation by an element of G); f is a product of elementary Nielsen-type automorphisms and is computed by a terminating procedure toStandardForm on words, primitive recursive when G = F(A) with word coefficients. Consequently V_G(W) is in bijection with V_G(f(W)) and the coordinate groups are G-isomorphic.
hypotheses: W strictly quadratic; for the procedure, G = F(A) with A finite and coefficients given as words.

nodes.title: Regular standard quadratic equations
nodes.statement: Let S = 1 be a standard quadratic equation over a freely discriminated group G (written r₁ ⋯ r_k d = 1). Put κ(S) = |X| + ε(S), with ε(S) = 1 when the coefficient d occurs and 0 otherwise. S = 1 is regular when it is [x, y] = d with d ≠ 1, or [x₁, y₁][x₂, y₂] = 1, or r(S) ≥ 2, S has a non-commutative solution and S is not of one of the types c₁^{z₁} c₂^{z₂} = c₁ c₂, x² c^z = a² c, x₁² x₂² = a₁² a₂². Equivalently, S is regular when κ(S) ≥ 4 and S has a non-commutative solution in G, or S is [x, y] d = 1.
proofSteps: A predicate combining the shape of S with the existence of a non-commutative solution.

nodes.title: Radicals of consistent standard quadratic equations
nodes.statement: Let G be freely discriminated (fully residually free, nonabelian or not) and S = 1 a standard quadratic equation over G with a solution in G. Then: (1) for S = [x, y] d or [x₁, y₁][x₂, y₂], R(S) = ncl(S); (2) for S = x² d, R(S) = ncl(x b) where b² = d; (3) for S = c^z d, R(S) = ncl([z b⁻¹, c]) where d⁻¹ = c^b; (4) for S = x₁² x₂², R(S) = ncl([x₁, x₂]); (5) for S = x₁² x₂² x₃², R(S) = ncl([x₁,x₂], [x₁,x₃], [x₂,x₃]); (6) if r(S) ≥ 2 and S has a non-commutative solution, R(S) = ncl(S); (7) if S is of type (4) and all its solutions are commutative, R(S) is the normal closure of the explicit system of commutation relations of IFT Theorem 2(7), and G_{R(S)} is an extension of a centralizer. In addition (general position) the equation has a solution in general position in the cases listed in IFT Theorem 1 (type (1) with n > 2, type (2) with n > 0 and n + m > 1, type (3) with n > 3, type (4) with n > 2, and r(S) ≥ 2 with a non-commutative solution).

nodes.title: Coordinate groups of regular quadratic equations as surface amalgams
nodes.statement: Let S = 1 be a regular standard quadratic equation of type (2) or (4) over a freely discriminated group G, with genus n and coefficients c₁, …, c_m, d. Then G_{R(S)} = G_S, and G_S is the fundamental group of the graph of groups with one vertex group G, one vertex group the surface group S±(n, m + 1) (orientable for type (2), non-orientable for type (4)), and m + 1 edges with infinite cyclic edge groups identifying the boundary elements p_j with conjugates of c_j (j ≤ m) and p_{m+1} with d (with the orientation fixed by the relator). For types (1) and (3), G_S = G ∗ S±(n, 0). The surface vertex is a QH vertex (FG6/qh-vertex) whose boundary subgroups are exactly the edge groups.
hypotheses: S regular (so R(S) = ncl(S) by FG6/quadratic-radicals (1), (6)).
proofSteps: G_S = (G ∗ F(X)) / ncl(S); rewriting S as the surface relator with p_j := z_j⁻¹ c_j z_j and p_{m+1} := d gives the amalgam presentation (Tietze moves), and FG4/one-edge-compatibility iterated identifies it with π₁ of the graph of groups.

nodes.title: Quadratically hanging (QH) vertices and their peripheral data
nodes.statement: Let T be an (𝒜, ℋ)-tree of a group G (FG4/tree-action). A vertex v is quadratically hanging (QH) when its stabilizer Q = G_v is an extension 1 → F → Q → π₁(Σ) → 1 with Σ a compact hyperbolic 2-orbifold (for the torsion-free CSA groups of this roadmap: F = 1 and Σ a compact surface with χ < 0 and π₁(Σ) a surface group S±(g, m)), such that every incident edge stabilizer and every Q ∩ g H g⁻¹ (H ∈ ℋ) is an extended boundary subgroup: its image in π₁(Σ) is finite or contained in a boundary subgroup. The peripheral data of v are the boundary subgroups of Σ, and a boundary component is used when its boundary subgroup contains with finite index the image of an incident edge stabilizer or of a conjugate of some H ∈ ℋ. Being QH is a property of a vertex in a given tree; rigidity and flexibility are defined relative to the splitting family in FG10.
proofSteps: A structure on a vertex of a G-tree recording F, Σ, the surjection and the extended-boundary condition.
acceptance: In the splitting of FG6/regular-quadratic-coordinate-group, the surface vertex is QH with Σ of genus n and m + 1 boundary components, all used.
A vertex group ℤ² is never QH (ℤ² is not an extension of a hyperbolic surface group by a fiber F = 1).

nodes.title: Generalised equations with constants and parameters
nodes.statement: A (combinatorial) generalised equation Ω over the basis A consists of: boundaries 1, …, ρ + 1 and items h₁, …, h_ρ (h_i between boundaries i and i + 1); a set of bases, each with left and right end-points α(μ) < β(μ), an orientation ε(μ) ∈ {±1}, and either a dual base Δ(μ) (with Δ(Δ(μ)) = μ, a variable base) or a label in A^{±1} (a constant base of length one); and boundary connections (p, μ, q) relating a boundary p inside μ to a boundary q inside Δ(μ). Its basic equations are h[α(μ), β(μ)]^{ε(μ)} = h[α(Δμ), β(Δμ)]^{ε(Δμ)}, its coefficient equations h_i = a for constant bases, and its boundary equations those of the boundary connections. A solution is a tuple U = (U₁, …, U_ρ) of nonempty reduced words over A^{±1} such that every side of every equation is reduced as written and the equations hold graphically; group solutions drop the reduced-as-written condition. Ω is formally consistent when the combinatorial conditions of IFT Definition 10 hold. A parametric generalised equation additionally partitions its closed sections into variable (active, non-active), parametric and constant sections, and is in standard form when these occur in that order. The coordinate group F_{R(Ω)} is the coordinate group (FG5) of the system of group equations Ω* over F(A).
proofSteps: A finite combinatorial structure (natural-number data), with decidable formal consistency (IFT Lemma 12).
acceptance: The generalised equation of IFT Fig. 2 has ten items h₁, …, h₁₀, eleven boundaries, basic equations h₁ = h₇, h₂ = h₈, h₅ = h₆, h₁h₂h₃h₄ = h₆h₇, h₅ = h₈h₉h₁₀ and coefficient equations h₃ = b, h₄ = a, h₉ = a, h₁₀ = b.

nodes.title: Reduction of systems of equations and inequations to generalised equations
nodes.statement: For an equation–inequation system (S, T) over F(A) (FG3/equation-system) with variables X, rewrite each inequation t ≠ 1 as the equation t z_t⁻¹ = 1 with a fresh variable z_t constrained to be nontrivial, and allow alphabet constraints (a variable required to lie in the subgroup generated by a sub-basis B ⊆ A, encoded by labels). proofSteps: Partition tables are bounded in size by a function of the total length of the system, hence finitely many and effectively enumerable (IFT Lemma 13).

nodes.statement: (1) If GE(S, T) is empty, (S, T) has no solution in F(A). nodes.title: Elementary and derived transformations of generalised equations
nodes.statement: The elementary transformations ET1 (cutting a base at a boundary connection), ET2 (transferring a base), ET3 (removing a pair of matched bases), ET4 (removing a linear base), ET5 (introducing a boundary) and the derived transformations D1–D6 (closing a section, transporting a closed section, completing a cut, moving free variables, linear elimination, tying a free boundary) associate to a formally consistent Ω a finite list of generalised equations Ω₁, …, Ω_r and surjective F-homomorphisms θ_i : F_{R(Ω)} → F_{R(Ω_i)} such that for every solution U of Ω there is a unique pair (Ω_i, U_i) with U = U_i ∘ θ_i. Each transformation has explicit applicability hypotheses; the exceptional cases of the sources are kept.

nodes.title: Makanin's finiteness theorem: a computable bound for minimal solutions
nodes.statement: There is a computable function f : ℕ → ℕ such that every formally consistent generalised equation Ω over a finite basis A (with alphabet constraints on items) that has a solution has one whose total length Σ |U_i| is at most f(‖Ω‖), where ‖Ω‖ is the size of the code of Ω. Consequently, for every equation–inequation system (S, T) over F(A) with alphabet constraints, if (S, T) has a solution then it has one of length at most a computable function of its size.
hypotheses: A finite; generalised equations formally consistent.
proofSteps: Exponent of periodicity: a minimal solution contains no subword P^k with k above a computable bound (Bulitko's lemma; IFT §5.4 periodic structures).

Makanin's process: applying the transformations of FG7/elementary-transformations with the complexity of the generalised equation, every infinite path in the process tree returns to an equation already seen (IFT Lemma 30) and type-12 and type-15 cycles are bounded by recursive functions on minimal solutions (IFT Lemmas 31–32); hence the tree T₀(Ω) traced by minimal solutions is finite and computable (IFT §5.5.3).
A solution of minimal length is read off a path of T₀(Ω) and its length is bounded in terms of the tree.
The proof uses neither the universal-theory decider nor any statement of FG10; IFT Lemma 15, which does use the universal theory, concerns isomorphism of coordinate groups and is not needed here.
Replacement route: RECOMP Corollary 1 gives an independent algorithm producing a finite graph of all solutions of equations with rational constraints over a free group, which yields the same bound.
acceptance: For x y x⁻¹ y⁻¹ = [a, b], a minimal solution is x = a, y = b, of total length 2.
For a system without solutions the statement is vacuous, and the solver must still prove unsatisfiability: that is the role of the bound.

nodes.title: Positive formulas as single equations (Malcev's equation)
nodes.statement: Let G be torsion-free, CSA, nonabelian and satisfying Vaught's condition ∀x∀y∀z (x² y² z² = 1 → [x,y] = [x,z] = [y,z] = 1) — in particular any nonabelian free group — and a, b ∈ G with [a, b] ≠ 1. (2) For equations S₁ = 1, …, S_k = 1 one effectively finds single equations S = 1 with V_G(S) = V_G(S₁, …, S_k) and S′ = 1 with V_G(S′) = V_G(S₁) ∪ … ∪ V_G(S_k). (3) Every positive quantifier-free formula of L_A is equivalent over G to a single equation, and every positive sentence to one of the form ∀x₁∃y₁ … ∀x_k∃y_k (S(X, Y, A) = 1), effectively.

(3) IFT Corollary 6 and the prenex form of §2.3 with fictitious quantifiers.

nodes.title: Merzljakov's theorem: formal solutions of positive sentences
nodes.statement: Let F = F(A) be a nonabelian free group of finite rank and S(X, Y, A) = 1 an equation with X = (x₁, …, x_k), Y = (y₁, …, y_k). If F ⊨ ∀x₁∃y₁ … ∀x_k∃y_k (S(X, Y, A) = 1), then there are words q₁(x₁), q₂(x₁, x₂), …, q_k(x₁, …, x_k) with q_i ∈ F[x₁, …, x_i] (the free product F ∗ F(x₁, …, x_i)) such that S(x₁, q₁(x₁), …, x_k, q_k(x₁, …, x_k), A) = 1 in F[X]: the equation has a solution in the free group F[X] whose i-th component depends only on x₁, …, x_i.
hypotheses: F nonabelian of finite rank; a single equation (by FG7/positive-normal-form every positive sentence reduces to this case).
proofSteps: Choose Merzljakov words g_i = b a^{m_{i1}} b ⋯ a^{m_{in_i}} b with increasing exponents, n_i larger than (max number of items of the members of GE(S)) · |S|, and no subword b a^{m} b shared with earlier g_l, h_l; choose h_i inductively so the remaining sentence holds.

Apply FG7/reduction-correct to the solution (g, h); each g_i contains a marked subword occurring inside a single item and exactly once; replace each marked occurrence b a^{m} b by b a^{m} x_i b throughout (IFT §4.4).

The modified tuple is a solution of the generalised equation over F[X] (the equations hold graphically), so X ↦ x_i, Y ↦ Q(Ũ) solves S over F[X]; the dependence of q_i on x₁, …, x_i comes from the marking order.
acceptance: For ∀x∃y (y = x a), the formal solution is q(x) = x a.
For ∀x∃y ([x, y] = 1) a formal solution is q(x) = x (or 1).

nodes.title: Residually free and fully residually free groups
nodes.statement: A group G is residually free when for every g ≠ 1 there are a free group F and a homomorphism φ : G → F with φ g ≠ 1, and fully residually free (freely discriminated, ω-residually free) when for every finite set g₁, …, g_n of nontrivial elements there are a free group F and φ : G → F with φ g_i ≠ 1 for all i. Free groups are quantified as Mathlib's IsFreeGroup over types in the universe of G (equivalently, by Nielsen–Schreier, FreeGroup (Fin 2) for countable G). For an F-group (F free nonabelian with fixed embedding) the coefficient version is FG5's F-discrimination by F.
proofSteps: Two predicates; the F-version is FG5/separation-discrimination with G = H = F.

nodes.title: Structure of fully residually free groups
nodes.statement: Let G be fully residually free. Then: (1) G is torsion-free, commutative transitive and CSA; (2) every finitely generated subgroup is fully residually free; (3) centralizers of nontrivial elements are abelian (maximal abelian subgroups are malnormal), and, for G finitely generated, every abelian subgroup is free abelian of finite rank, so centralizers are free abelian of finite rank but need not be cyclic; (4) two elements generate 1, ℤ, ℤ² or a nonabelian free group of rank 2; (5) a nonabelian fully residually free group is a domain (FG5).
proofSteps: (1), (2), (4): LIMITS Proposition 3.1, by transferring finitely many relations or non-relations to a free quotient.

(3) Abelian subgroups embed, through discriminating maps, in centralizers of free groups (FG1/centralizer-cyclic) only for finitely many elements at a time, so they are torsion-free abelian; finite generation of abelian subgroups of finitely generated fully residually free groups uses the embedding of FG8/embedding-theorems (SUBGROUPS Lemma 20).
(5) FG5/domain-examples.
acceptance: In ℤ² ∗ ℤ, a fully residually free group, the centralizer of (1,0) is ℤ²: centralizers are abelian but not cyclic.
The free-group statement ‘centralizers are cyclic’ (FG1/centralizer-cyclic) fails for limit groups, as ℤ² shows.

nodes.title: The space of marked groups and limit groups
nodes.statement: For n ∈ ℕ, the space 𝒢_n of n-marked groups is the set of normal subgroups of FreeGroup (Fin n), topologised as a closed subset of the Cantor space Set (FreeGroup (Fin n)) = 2^{F_n} (product topology); a marked group (G, S) with S : Fin n → G generating G corresponds to the kernel of FreeGroup.lift S. A limit group is a finitely generated group G some (equivalently every) marking of which is a limit in 𝒢_n of markings of free groups.
proofSteps: Topology induced from the product topology on Set (FreeGroup (Fin n)); normal subgroups form a closed, hence compact, subset.

nodes.title: Extensions of centralizers and iterated extensions
nodes.statement: For a group G, u ∈ G and n ≥ 1, the extension of the centralizer of u by ℤⁿ is G(u, ℤⁿ) := G ∗_{C_G(u)} (C_G(u) × ℤⁿ), the amalgam (Monoid.PushoutI) of G and C_G(u) × ℤⁿ along C_G(u); for n = 1 it is the HNN extension ⟨G, t | [c, t] = 1, c ∈ C_G(u)⟩. nodes.statement: Let G be a nonabelian CSA group with the big powers property (in particular a nonabelian fully residually free group) and u ∈ G not a proper power. nodes.title: Embedding theorems and finite presentability
nodes.statement: (1) (Kharlampovich–Myasnikov) A finitely generated group is fully residually free if and only if it embeds in Lyndon's group F^{ℤ[x]}; equivalently it embeds in an iterated extension of centralizers over a free group of finite rank. (2) Every finitely generated residually free group embeds in a direct product of finitely many fully residually free groups. (3) Every finitely generated fully residually free group is finitely presented, and so is every finitely generated subgroup of it (they are themselves fully residually free). (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of an ICE group over F is built from free abelian groups of finite rank by finitely many free products, amalgams over abelian groups one of which is maximal abelian, free extensions of centralizers, and separated HNN extensions with abelian associated subgroups one of which is maximal abelian.
proofSteps: (1) VAR-II Theorems 3–4: irreducible coordinate groups embed in coordinate groups of nondegenerate TQ systems, which embed in ICE groups (VAR-II Theorem 1), and conversely ICE groups are discriminated (FG8/centralizer-extension-discriminated).
(2) VAR-II Corollary 2, via FG5/noetherian-components (the coordinate group embeds in the product over the irreducible components).

nodes.title: Triangular quasi-quadratic and NTQ systems
nodes.statement: Over a group G, a triangular quasi-quadratic (TQ) system is a finite system S = S₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ S_n in disjoint tuples of variables X₁, …, X_n where each S_i(X_i, …, X_n, G) is of one of the types: (1) a standard quadratic equation in X_i with coefficients in G_{i+1} := G_{R(S_{i+1}, …, S_n)} (quadratic level); (2) commutation equations [x, y] = 1, [x, u] = 1 for x, y ∈ X_i and u in a finite set U_i ⊆ G_{i+1} generating a centralizer of G_{i+1} (centralizer-extension level); (3) [x, y] = 1 for x, y ∈ X_i (free abelian level); (4) the empty system (free level). With G_{n+1} := G, S is nondegenerate (NTQ) when each S_i = 1 has a solution in G_{i+1} (with X_{i+1}, … as constants). The coordinate group G_{R(S)} of an NTQ system is an NTQ group. An NTQ system is regular when each level is of type (1) with S_i in standard form and regular (FG6/regular-quadratic) or of type (4).
proofSteps: A structure listing the levels with their types and coefficient data; nondegeneracy as a Prop referring to FG5 coordinate groups of the lower levels.

nodes.title: Lyndon length functions: free and regular
nodes.statement: Let Λ be an ordered abelian group and G a group. A Lyndon length function is l : G → Λ with (L1) l(1) = 0; (L2) l(g⁻¹) = l(g); (L3) c(g, f) > c(g, h) → c(g, h) = c(f, h) for all g, f, h, where the Gromov product c(g, f) = ½(l(g) + l(f) − l(g⁻¹ f)) is taken in the divisible hull Λ ⊗ ℚ. It is free when moreover (L4) c(g, f) ∈ Λ for all g, f and (L5) l(g²) > l(g) for g ≠ 1; it is regular when (L6) for all g, f there are u, g₁, f₁ with g = u ∘ g₁, f = u ∘ f₁ and l(u) = c(g, f), where x = y ∘ z means x = y z and l(x) = l(y) + l(z). Freeness and regularity are independent properties.
proofSteps: A structure with a function to Λ and the axioms; Gromov products valued in the divisible hull (Mathlib's ℚ-module of a torsion-free abelian group, or Λ ⊗ ℚ).

nodes.title: Infinite words over an ordered abelian group
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a discretely ordered abelian group (least positive element 1) and X a set. An infinite (Λ-)word is a function w : [1, α_w] → X^{±1} on the interval [1, α_w] = {β ∈ Λ | 1 ≤ β ≤ α_w}, α_w ≥ 0, with |w| := α_w; it is reduced when w(β + 1) ≠ w(β)⁻¹. R(Λ, X) is the set of reduced Λ-words with the partial multiplication u ∗ v (defined when the maximal common initial segment com(u⁻¹, v) exists, removing it), and inversion. CDR(Λ, X) is the subset of words admitting a cyclic decomposition c⁻¹ ∘ v ∘ c with v cyclically reduced. For Λ = ℤ, R(ℤ, X) is the set of reduced words and ∗ is the multiplication of FreeGroup X.

nodes.title: Universal ellipticity, JSJ trees and the JSJ deformation space
nodes.statement: Fix a group G, a family 𝒜 of subgroups closed under conjugation and taking subgroups (cyclic, or abelian), and a finite family ℋ of subgroups. Among (𝒜, ℋ)-trees (FG4/tree-action): a subgroup is universally elliptic when it is elliptic in every (𝒜, ℋ)-tree, and a tree is universally elliptic when its edge stabilizers are. A JSJ tree is a universally elliptic (𝒜, ℋ)-tree dominating every universally elliptic (𝒜, ℋ)-tree; the JSJ deformation space is the set of JSJ trees (when nonempty it is one deformation space over the universally elliptic groups of 𝒜). A vertex stabilizer of a JSJ tree is rigid when it is elliptic in every (𝒜, ℋ)-tree and flexible otherwise. Two JSJ decompositions are equivalent when they lie in the same deformation space; no single displayed graph of groups is canonical.
proofSteps: Predicates on (𝒜, ℋ)-trees defined from FG4's ellipticity and domination.

nodes.title: Effective relative Grushko decompositions
nodes.statement: There is a procedure which, for a promised input G (finitely generated fully residually free, by a finite presentation) and a finite family ℋ of finitely generated subgroups (by generating sets), decides whether G has a nontrivial free decomposition relative to ℋ (each H ∈ ℋ in a factor) and, iterating, computes a Grushko decomposition G = G₁ ∗ ⋯ ∗ G_p ∗ F_q relative to ℋ: finite generating sets of the factors (as words in the generators of G), finite presentations of the factors, and the isomorphism data. It is computable and halts on the promised class, and its output is correct up to the uniqueness of FG4/kurosh-grushko (factors up to conjugacy and permutation).
hypotheses: Promised input class; ℋ finite family of finitely generated subgroups.
proofSteps: JSJ Theorem 10.1 decides the existence of a free decomposition with H in a factor, using the elimination process on generalised equations of FG7 and the algorithms of FG10/frf-basic-algorithms; induction on the rank (Grushko–Neumann, FG4/kurosh-grushko) bounds the iteration.
acceptance: For G = ℤ² ∗ F(c, d) the output has p = 1 (G₁ = ℤ²), q = 2.

nodes.title: Effective cyclic and abelian JSJ decompositions
nodes.statement: There is a procedure which, for a promised input G (finitely generated, freely indecomposable relative to ℋ, fully residually free) and a finite family ℋ of finitely generated subgroups, computes a cyclic (respectively abelian) JSJ decomposition of G relative to ℋ: a finite graph of groups with explicit vertex groups (generators as words in G, finite presentations), edge groups with their monomorphisms (as images of generators), the identification of G with π₁ (images of the generators of G and of π₁), and the labelling of vertices as rigid, abelian or QH with the surface data of each QH vertex. It is computable and halts on the promised class; its output lies in the JSJ deformation space (FG10/jsj-existence), so it is correct up to equivalence of JSJ decompositions, not as a literal displayed graph.

nodes.title: Makanin–Razborov (Hom-) diagrams
nodes.statement: For a finitely generated group G and the free group F, a Hom(G, F)-diagram (Makanin–Razborov diagram) is a finite rooted tree with: the root labelled G; every other vertex v labelled by a finitely generated fully residually free group G_v (given by a finite presentation) with a modular group Mod(G_v) ≤ Aut(G_v) (generated by Dehn twists along edges of its abelian JSJ decomposition, automorphisms of its QH vertex groups fixing the peripheral structure, and automorphisms of abelian vertex groups fixing the peripheral subgroups); every edge labelled by a homomorphism (from the root: a homomorphism G → G_v; otherwise a proper epimorphism G_v ↠ G_w); and every leaf labelled by a free group (a free product of F with a free group in the coefficient version). A branch B: G → G_{v₁} → ⋯ → G_{v_k} = F_B together with σ_i ∈ Mod(G_{v_i}) and a homomorphism ψ : F_B → F gives the composite homomorphism ψ ∘ π_k ∘ σ_k ∘ ⋯ ∘ π₁ ∘ σ₁ ∘ π₀ (the branch restrictions, if any, are part of the data). The diagram is complete when every homomorphism G → F is such a composite; the F-version uses F-homomorphisms.
proofSteps: A finite tree datatype with group presentations, homomorphisms on generators and generating sets of modular groups.
acceptance: For the empty system over F (G = F[X]), the one-edge diagram with leaf F[X] and the identity is F-complete: every solution is a specialisation of the leaf.

For S = [x, a] = 1 over F(a,b): the root is F_{R(S)} = ⟨F, t | [a, t]⟩ (x = t) with modular group generated by the twist t ↦ t a, and one edge to the leaf F by t ↦ 1; the composites are t ↦ a^k, exactly the solutions.

sources.match: Complete canonical Hom(G, F)- and Hom_F(G, F)-diagrams, effectively constructed for finitely presented G; for a finite system S, the solutions of S in F are exactly the F-homomorphisms of the diagram.

nodes.title: Effective Makanin–Razborov diagrams: soundness and completeness
nodes.statement: There is a computable procedure which, for every finite system S(X) = 1 over a free group F of finite rank (word coefficients), halts and returns an F-complete Hom_F(F_{R(S)}, F)-diagram C such that: (soundness) every branch composite is an F-homomorphism F_{R(S)} → F, i.e. a solution of S; (completeness) every solution of S in F factors as a branch composite (through an allowed branch, with modular automorphisms and a final specialisation of the leaf). Edges below the root are proper epimorphisms between finitely generated fully residually free groups, so every branch is finite; the leaves are F ∗ (free group).
hypotheses: F free of finite rank; S finite with word coefficients.
proofSteps: Build the solution tree T_sol(Ω, Λ) of the generalised equations of FG7/reduction-to-generalized-equations (IFT §5.6, Theorems 5–7); every solution is a composition along a path (IFT Theorem 5).

Replace coordinate groups by their maximal fully residually free quotients and compute modular groups from effective JSJ decompositions (JSJ §11, using FG10/effective-jsj); finiteness from the descending chain condition for limit groups (proper epimorphisms terminate: LIMITS Proposition 3.13).
Soundness is by construction (composites of homomorphisms); completeness from IFT Theorem 5 and JSJ Theorem 11.3.
acceptance: For S = [x, y] = 1 over F, the diagram's branches give all commuting pairs (u^m, u^n) after specialisation.

nodes.statement: There is a computable procedure which, for a finitely generated fully residually free group H given by a finite presentation (promised input) and a finite system S(X) = 1 with coefficients in H (as words in the generators of H), decides whether S has a solution in H and returns one if it exists; moreover a complete Hom_H(H_{R(S)}, H)-diagram can be computed. nodes.title: Compatible equations, S-lifts and complete S-lifts
nodes.statement: Let G be a group, S(X) = 1 a system over G with a solution in G, and μ : G[X] → G_{R(S)} the canonical map. A formula Φ(X, Y) of L_A (in particular T(X, Y) = 1, or T(X, Y) = 1 ∧ W(X, Y) ≠ 1) is compatible with S over G when for every solution a of S in G there is b with Φ(a, b) true in G (V_G(S) is the projection of the truth set of Φ ∧ S = 1). A compatible Φ admits an S-lift (a lift to a generic point) when ∃Y Φ(X^μ, Y) is true in G_{R(S)}, the elements X^μ treated as constants; a solution Y(X) ∈ G_{R(S)}^{|Y|} is a formal solution. A compatible equation T(X, Y) = 1 admits a complete S-lift when every formula T = 1 ∧ W ≠ 1 compatible with S admits an S-lift. A family Θ of solutions of S is generic when every equation V(X, Y) = 1 such that V(X^θ, Y) = 1 is solvable in G for all θ ∈ Θ admits a complete S-lift.
proofSteps: Predicates on systems and formulas, using FG5 coordinate groups and FG3 formulas.
acceptance: Over F, T = (y² = x²) is compatible with the empty system S and admits the lift y = x.
Over F, T = (y² = x) is not compatible with the empty system (x = a has no square root).

nodes.title: Compatibility and lifts in terms of coordinate groups
nodes.statement: Let S(X) = 1 have a solution in G. (1) T(X, Y) = 1 is compatible with S over G iff G_{R(S)} embeds canonically in G_{R(S ∪ T)} and every G-homomorphism G_{R(S)} → G extends to G_{R(S ∪ T)}. (2) T is compatible with S and admits an S-lift iff there is a G-retraction G_{R(S ∪ T)} → G_{R(S)} (identity on G_{R(S)}); a solution of T(X^μ, Y) = 1 in G_{R(S)} gives the retraction and conversely. (3) If G_{R(S)} is G-discriminated by G, a compatible T admits an S-lift as soon as T(X^θ, Y) = 1 is solvable for all θ in a discriminating family — this is how generic families are used.
proofSteps: (1) LIFT Proposition 2.5; (2) LIFT Proposition 2.8; (3) IFT Lemmas 36–40 and Propositions 2–3 (separating families and lifts).
acceptance: For S empty, (2) says T admits a lift iff F[X] is a retract of F_{R(T)} over F[X].

nodes.title: The basic sequence of automorphisms of a regular quadratic equation
nodes.statement: For a regular standard orientable quadratic equation S(X) = 1 over G (genus n, coefficients c₁, …, c_m, d), the basic sequence Γ = (γ₁, …, γ_K), K = K(m, n) (K = m + 4n − 1 when m, n ≠ 0, 4n − 1 when m = 0), consists of G-automorphisms of G[X] fixing the left side of S, each a Dehn twist of the surface splitting of FG6/regular-quadratic-coordinate-group along a simple closed curve of a fixed chain of curves. For a tuple p = (p₁, …, p_K) of positive integers, φ_{K,p} := γ_K^{p_K} ⋯ γ₁^{p₁}; the same construction with the curve system of a non-orientable surface gives the basic automorphisms of non-orientable regular equations.
hypotheses: S regular, in standard form.
proofSteps: Define each γ_i on the generators X by the explicit formulas of IFT §7.1 (Nielsen-type substitutions conjugating a block of variables by a product of atoms); check that γ_i fixes S, i.e. is a Dehn twist (FG4/dehn-twist) of the surface vertex.

nodes.title: Generic families of solutions of regular quadratic equations
nodes.statement: Let G be a finitely generated fully residually free group, S = 1 a regular standard orientable quadratic equation over G, Γ its basic sequence and β : G_S → G a solution in general position. For any J ≥ 2 and any unbounded set P ⊆ ℕ^{JK}, the family Ξ_{P,β} = {φ_{JK,p} β | p ∈ P} G-discriminates G_{R(S)} into G, and so does Ξ_{P,β,p′} = {φ_{tK,p′} θ | θ ∈ Ξ_{P,β}} for any fixed p′; these families are generic in the sense of FG11/compatibility-and-lifts. The analogous statement holds for non-orientable regular equations with their basic automorphisms.
hypotheses: G finitely generated fully residually free; S regular; β in general position (exists by FG6/quadratic-radicals).
proofSteps: Big powers and the Nielsen property of φ_{K,p} with respect to the words of Γ (IFT Lemmas 42–65, §7.2–7.3): long products of large powers do not cancel.
G_{R(S)} embeds in an extension of centralizers of G (LIFT Propositions 5.1–5.2), discriminated by FG8/centralizer-extension-discriminated.
acceptance: For S = [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] over F, the solutions φ_{K,p}(a, b, b, a) with p large discriminate F ∗ S⁺(2, 0).

nodes.title: Implicit function theorem for regular quadratic equations
nodes.statement: Let S(X, A) = 1 be a regular standard quadratic equation over F = F(A). Every equation T(X, Y, A) = 1 compatible with S over F admits a complete S-lift: for every W(X, Y) such that T = 1 ∧ W ≠ 1 is compatible with S, there is Y(X) ∈ F_{R(S)}^{|Y|} (words in X ∪ A modulo R(S) = ncl(S)) with T(X, Y(X)) = 1 and W(X, Y(X)) ≠ 1 in F_{R(S)}. The lift is effective: FG11/lift-procedure computes it. The statement extends to finitely generated fully residually free coefficient groups G in place of F where the source proves it (IFT Corollary 12).
hypotheses: S regular standard quadratic over F; T compatible with S (and W such that T ∧ W ≠ 1 is compatible).
proofSteps: Apply the solution tree of T ∧ S with parameters X to the generic family of FG11/generic-families; cut equations (IFT §5.7, LIFT Theorem 3.4) show that for large p the solutions over the generic family factor through a single branch whose values are words in X (IFT §7.4, proof of Theorem 9).
The inequality W ≠ 1 is preserved by choosing the branch where W does not vanish on the discriminating family (IFT p. 135).
acceptance: For S = [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] and T = (z = x₁ y₁), the lift is z = x₁ y₁ (trivially).
For S = [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] and T = ([z, x₁] = 1 ∧ z ≠ 1), a lift is z = x₁.

nodes.title: Implicit function theorem for regular NTQ systems
nodes.statement: Let U(X, A) = 1 be a regular NTQ system over F = F(A) (every level a regular standard quadratic equation or empty). Every equation V(X, Y, A) = 1 compatible with U admits a complete U-lift, effectively. When U is entirely empty this is Merzljakov's theorem in the form with inequations (formal solutions in F[X]). The claim is not extended to NTQ systems with non-regular quadratic levels, abelian levels or centralizer-extension levels.
hypotheses: U regular NTQ; V compatible with U.
proofSteps: Induction on the number of levels (IFT proof of Theorem 11): build the solution tree of V ∧ U with parameters X = X₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ X_n; on the top level use FG11/ift-regular-quadratic (or Merzljakov words for empty levels, FG7/merzljakov-theorem); lift level by level through the coordinate groups of FG8/ntq-coordinate-group.
acceptance: For U the two-level system with level 1: [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] = z (coefficients from level 2) and level 2 empty in z, a compatible V lifts by combining Merzljakov words for z with the quadratic theorem.
